//: The complete set of what this webview may ask the shell to do.
Tauri 2 denies anything not listed here. That is the point of the file: an
empty capabilities directory means a shell the page cannot reach at all,
which is the correct starting point for a template.
Three permissions, and each one is a capability the front end actually uses:
* `opener:allow-open-url` — hand ONE approval URL to the user's own
browser. Deliberately not `opener:default`: the opener plugin's default
set includes launching applications and revealing files, neither of which
this app needs.
* `stronghold:default` — create, read and delete records in the vault the
opt-in 'remember me' uses. There is no network permission, no
peer-to-peer permission, and no procedure execution: the front end stores
a session token and reads it back, and cannot ask the vault to do
anything else.
What is NOT here, and why each absence matters:
* No `path:` permission, and no path plugin in Cargo.toml. The front end
does not choose where the vault snapshot lives; one application command
resolves the application's own data directory and returns it. A page that
could name a path could aim the vault anywhere.
`core:default` is the framework's own baseline (event system, window,
application lifecycle). It grants no filesystem, shell or network access.
What is NOT here, and why each absence matters:
* No `shell:` permission. The snapshot's launcher could open remote URLs
and run commands; a compromised dependency inherited both.
* No `http:` permission. The front end reaches the API with the platform
`fetch`, and the CSP names that one origin.
* No updater and no sidecar. Both need an endpoint, a keypair or a binary
that belongs to whoever ships this app.
